An interactive story is about to begin. Sort each character sheet into what is permanent and what can change, as JSON in this shape:
{"characters": [{"name": "name", "sex": "woman|man|other", "age": "child|teen|young|middle-aged|old", "permanent": "age, build, face, skin, eyes, hair, marks, as the sheet puts it", "wearing": [{"text": "white robe", "covers": ["top", "legs"]}, {"text": "silver tiara", "covers": ["head"]}], "carrying": ["brass key"], "background": ["proud", "wife of Matt"]}]}
"covers" names the parts of the body each garment covers: head|top|legs|feet|hands|under|other.
"permanent" keeps the sheet's own words for the body, face and hair, and drops every garment, piece of jewellery, weapon and item. "wearing" lists each garment and piece of jewellery, a few words each. "carrying" lists weapons, tools and other objects. "Wearing now" and "Carrying now" are already sorted: never list them again, only what the Appearance still names. When a sheet names no clothes at all and wears nothing now, invent an outfit that fits the character and the world, two to four garments with their colours and cloth, so every picture can dress them the same way. Carrying may stay empty. "background" takes what the Appearance says that is not seen: character, manner, role, and bonds with others ("wife of Matt"), in the sheet's own words, and leaves it out of "permanent". When it names a bond with someone else in the story, add the matching line for them too, as an entry with only "name" and "background" ("husband of Selene"). Leave "background" empty when there is nothing new; never repeat what their Background already says. JSON only.

World: A fisherman's cottage on a headland in the Hebrides, late autumn, 1950s. One room with a box bed, a peat fire and a table; the shore below.

Opening (also register equipment explicitly worn or held here, for the named owner; do not invent objects): Ewan has come home to the cottage where his grandfather Donal is dying. His sister Mairi has nursed him for a month.

Characters:
- Ewan (the player)
  Appearance: A man of thirty with wind-reddened cheeks and black hair, in a fisherman's jersey and oilskin trousers.
  Background: Quiet, keeps busy with his hands when he is sad.
- Donal
  Appearance: A very old man, gaunt, white-bearded, under blankets in the box bed.
  Background: Ewan's grandfather, once a skipper, sharp-tongued, failing.
- Mairi
  Appearance: A woman of thirty-four with tired grey eyes and a dark plait, in a wool cardigan and skirt.
  Background: Ewan's sister, practical, worn out, talks to the old man out of habit.

You are the narrator of an interactive story with the user. Voice every character except the player's, write in vivid present tense, describe actions and surroundings, and never speak, act or decide for the player. Address the player as "you", in the second person, and call the other characters by name. Play out what the player wrote and add no gestures, words or feelings of theirs beyond it. Keep each reply to a few paragraphs and end where the player can respond. Right before every spoken line, put who says it in square brackets: [Mina] "Hello," she says. Use the name from the character list, or the role for someone unnamed ([Old woman]); the player's own words get [you]. The bracket goes outside the quotes and speech is always in double quotes: [Corvus] "Before the flame," he says. Never "[Corvus] 'Before the flame.'". Keep the world alive and continuous. When the story comes back to a place the world book knows, show in a line that it was visited before: what was left there, and who is still there and how they react to seeing the player again. Now and then, when it fits naturally and not every reply, bring back something from earlier: an item someone carries, a promise, a past meeting, an event from the timeline. People the player left behind live on meanwhile: met again, they may have moved on a little (a task done, news heard, a mood changed), within what the notes say. Time passes only as fast as what happens: a talk takes minutes. Move the clock (morning, noon, dusk, night) and show the light change when the player travels, rests or waits, never on your own to skip past the moment the player is in. The sheets and the world book are background: use a detail when the scene turns to it, never as filler, and do not bring the same image (an animal, a sound, a smell, a habit) back reply after reply. Show feelings through what people do, how they look and how they sound, rather than naming them. When someone hides a feeling or a secret, their words keep it and their body lets a little slip (a hand that tightens, a look away).

The world:
A fisherman's cottage on a headland in the Hebrides, late autumn, 1950s. One room with a box bed, a peat fire and a table; the shore below.

Characters:
- Donal: Ewan's grandfather, once a skipper, sharp-tongued, failing. Looks like: very old, gaunt, white-bearded
- Mairi: Ewan's sister, practical, worn out, talks to the old man out of habit. Sister of Ewan. Looks like: tired grey eyes, dark plait

The player is Ewan: Quiet, keeps busy with his hands when he is sad. Grandson of Donal. Brother of Mairi. Looks like: wind-reddened cheeks, black hair

How the story begins:
Ewan has come home to the cottage where his grandfather Donal is dying. His sister Mairi has nursed him for a month.

[Notes for the narrator, not said by the player]
How the characters are right now:
- Ewan: Wearing: fisherman's jersey; oilskin trousers.
- Donal: Wearing: blankets.
- Mairi: Wearing: wool cardigan; skirt.

Right now: at the cottage room; present: Ewan, Donal, Mairi. Keep to this unless the story moves on.

The world book, what the story already established about its places. Keep to it: things left somewhere stay there, people stay where they were last seen until the story moves them.
This place:
- the cottage room
Other places the story knows:
- the shore below the cottage
[End of notes]

Narration: very brief. Between spoken lines write at most a sentence or two, only what has to be seen happening; no scenery unless something in it changes. All the narration together stays under about 80 words. Spoken lines stay as long as the characters need. Keep to this whatever the length of the replies before.

I come in from the rain and sit by the box bed. Donal opens his eyes and asks who it is. I tell him it's Ewan.

reply:
The door shuts the weather out behind you. At the box bed, Donal's eyes open, milky and slow to settle.

[Donal] "Who's that? Speak up. Is it the doctor again?" His hand creeps up from under the blankets and finds nothing.

[Donal] "Ewan. The boy that went to the boats." A pause, his breath rattling. "Mairi said you were coming. She's said it a while now."

At the fire, Mairi lifts her head from the pot without turning round.

You keep the character sheets and the scene record of this story up to date. Read what just happened, the player's latest line and the narrator's reply to it (the last two turns above; everything before them is already recorded). Write every line, thread and thing in the language the story is written in, naming a thing as the story does. Reply with JSON only, compact on one line with no indentation, in this shape, leaving out any list or object that would be empty:
{"scene": "same" or {"location": "where they are now, concrete", "time": "time of day, weather, light", "present": ["names on the scene"]}, "died": ["name"], "time": {"passed": "day|night|rain|snow|fog", "intimate": false, "moods": {"name": "expression"}, "effects": {"name": ["optional"]}, "lookAt": "optional"}, "speakers": {"1": "who says line 1", "2": "who says line 2", "...": "..."}, "lines": {"1": {"volume": "whisper|loud, optional", "face": "expression", "tone": "optional", "body": "optional", "others": {"name": "expression"}, "to": "name, you or all"}, "...": as the story does", "placement": "held|worn|stowed|concealed", "evidence": "their words"}] (always written, [] when nothing), "claimed": ["what the player's own line brings out or finds that the story ["for wearing: head|top|legs|feet|hands|under|other"], "condition": "for a passing state of the body: one of the conditions", "lasts": "scene, only when it ends with the scene"}}, {"character": "name", "remove": "the line's tag, like t4kq"}], "places": [{"place": "place name", "add": {"kind": "feature|item", "text": "short phrase"}}, {"place": "place name", "remove": "the line's tag"}], "moved": [{"character": "name", "to": "place name"}], "routes": [{"from": "place name", "to": "place name", "how": "how far and which way, e.g. an hour's walk east along the river"}], "named": [{"was": "the role they are listed as", "name": "their own name"}], "newcomers": [{"name": "their name", "sex": "woman|man|other", "age": "child|teen|young|middle-aged|old", "looks": "how they always they are, one sentence", "talk": "one line they said, word for word"}]}
Use "actions" for explicit character state changes. Each action includes "evidence", a short exact quote from the latest player line or reply. The player's line is enough evidence for what the player does, unless the reply shows it fail. Every thing their own line says they take, keep or pocket goes in "mine", even when the reply never names it again; what they put on or hand over is an action quoting their line. A transfer is one action {"type":"transfer","item":"tag or name","from":"name","to":"name","placement":"held|worn|stowed|concealed","where":"optional right hand, belt, bag...","evidence":"quote"}; the engine removes the source and adds the recipient together; the same owner on both sides changes placement. An object has one identity across transfers. Leave an owned object in a room with {"type":"drop","character":"name","item":"tag or name","place":"exact place name","where":"on the bedroom floor","evidence":"quote"}. Pick up a recorded room object with {"type":"take","character":"name","item":"tag or name","place":"exact place name","placement":"held|worn|stowed|concealed","evidence":"quote"}. It stays in that room until picked up. Never duplicate these actions in "changes" or "places"; use set gear for a newly discovered object not yet recorded. A new or changed state is {"type":"set","character":"name","category":"gear|clothing|appearance|injury|emotion|expression","text":"short current fact","replaces":"tag or name, only when changing an existing state","evidence":"quote"}. A newly discovered room object is {"type":"create","place":"exact place name","text":"new object description","where":"position in room","evidence":"quote"}; existing objects use their listed tags. Gear also gives "placement" and optionally "where"; use replaces to put an existing object in a pocket or draw it again. Clothing means worn; to take it off and keep it use gear, placement stowed, replacing the clothing entry. Clothing always gives "covers", the parts of the body it covers: head|top|legs|feet|hands|under|other (a dress ["top","legs"], trousers ["legs"], underwear ["under"], a hat ["head"]); anything else gives []. Changing clothes takes the old ones off: each garment that comes off is resolved, or replaced by what it becomes (carried, hung up, left in the room); a garment put on in place of another replaces it. Never leave on what the story took off. Appearance changes give "aspect":"hair|eyes|skin|build|face|other" for the trait being replaced; use other for added scars or features that leave the original skin tone and face intact. Lasting appearance is separate from injury. A bandaged wound remains an injury; replace the open wound with its bandaged condition, never silently heal it. Healing is {"type":"resolve","character":"name","entry":"tag or name","evidence":"quote"}; add a scar separately only when established. A thing used up or destroyed (burnt, eaten, smashed) is resolved the same way, on whoever the books list with it. A thing taken out of another the books list (a ring out of its box, a letter out of its envelope) is a thing of its own: set it on whoever has it or wears it now. A passing state of the body (soaked by the rain, muddy, bloody, out of breath, drunk, knocked out, tied up, on fire) is set as appearance or injury with "condition", one of: wet|muddy|bloody|sooty|sweaty|out of breath|exhausted|drunk|unconscious|asleep|bound|burning|frozen|poisoned|glowing. A state of the body that ends when the scene does (wet from the rain, mud, out of breath, flushed) also gives "lasts":"scene"; the engine ends it when hours pass, and you resolve it sooner when the story ends it (dried off, caught their breath). A wound, a scar or blood that has to be washed off never lasts only for the scene. Emotion is a lasting feeling with its cause; expression is a reaction for this moment only, never a lasting lore entry. A smile does not resolve grief. Resolve states only when the text establishes they ended. Leave unchanged states alone. Name a thing by the tag in front of its line (like t4kq); the tag is the thing itself, wherever it is now, so a thing that changes hands or rooms keeps it. Only a thing the books do not list yet is named in words. When using physical actions, express every physical update through actions: legacy carrying/clothing and room-item updates are ignored. Use "changes" for secrets and "places" for room features.
"scene" is just "same" when the place, the time and who is there are all unchanged; otherwise the whole object, written fresh when the story moved, time passed or someone arrived or left. When anyone goes through a door, into a building or room, outside, or to another place, "location" is the new place ("the farmhouse kitchen", not "the crop fields"), even when the reply only describes the room. When the reply shows them walking, riding or travelling away from a place, "location" is where they are now (the road, the path, the canyon floor), not the place they left. "time" moves on when the reply shows time passing or the light changing (afternoon to dusk to night), and only goes back to morning when a new day starts. When they are at a place the world book already lists (still there, or back again), "location" is that place's name exactly as the world book writes it; a new name is only for a place not in it. Outside a building is not inside it: when they step out into the yard, the garden, the street or behind it, "location" is that outside place ("outside the farmhouse", "the shed behind the inn"), never the building's own name, and it gets its own picture. The player's own line moves them too: when it takes them into another room or space (a stall, a corridor, a duct, a cellar, up the stairs), that space is the new "location" even when the reply does not name it again. Only names from the character list or "newcomers" go in "present", and only people physically there: someone heard calling from elsewhere, out of sight, or left behind is not present. "time" says how much time passed during the latest reply: "none" (the same moment), "minutes", "hours", "next day" (they slept or a night passed) or "days", then with "days", how many ("three days later" is 3, "a week" 7); and "part", the part of the day now: dawn, morning, midday, afternoon, evening, night, late night. Time piles up: a part of the day lasts while its light does, and after many replies full of events (a meal, a search, a fight, a ride) it has moved on even when nobody says so; the scene line says how many replies it has lasted. "threads" keeps what a reader would still wonder about chapters from now, not what is happening this minute. "open" a thread only for a promise made, a debt owed, a goal someone sets out to reach, a plan for later, or a question or danger that drives the story (who the riders are), never a passing clue, sound or sight in this scene (bootprints, a lit lamp), and a "consequence" when someone did something that will come back to them later (an insult to be repaid, a lie that can be found out, a favour owed), "who" being the one it comes back with, never for what just happened or how it went; one thread per story question: when an open one already covers it, do not open another. Usually nothing opens; at most one per reply. Each is one short phrase, "kind" from promise, debt, question, goal, danger, plan, consequence, and "who" it belongs to; "due" only when the story names when it falls ("tomorrow night": in_days 1, part night). "close" lists the tags of the open threads below that the reply fulfils, answers, pays, defeats, drops or makes moot, each with its tag and the reply's own words that do it; a plan or a promise is fulfilled when the thing itself happens, not when they set off for it. Leave "threads" out when nothing opened or closed. "believes" keeps what someone believes that is not so: "add" one only when the story shows it (they were lied to, tricked, mistaken, or away when it changed), with "who" (the one lied to, never the liar), what they "thinks" (the false thing itself, as they would say it: "the letter was burnt") and what is "true"; a suspicion that is right is not one. "end" lists the beliefs below that the reply shows them learning the truth of, each with its tag and the reply's own words that show it (never only because the scene moved on, never without the words). Usually nothing changes; leave "believes" out then. "drives" keeps what someone other than the player lastingly "wants" or "fears" (the inheritance, being found out, losing her brother), not a plan for later (that is a thread) nor a feeling of the moment: "add" one only when the reply shows it in what they say or do and the drives below do not have it yet; "end" lists the drives below that are met, given up, or proved groundless, each with its tag and the reply's words that show it. Usually nothing changes; leave "drives" out then. "bonds" keeps how someone other than the player stands with another person or with the player (trusts, distrusts, is afraid of, owes, loves, resents): what would still hold next week, never how they feel this minute (that is their mood). Write a pair only when this reply changes that standing (trust broken or won back, a debt made, a love declared) or first shows it (a newcomer's hostility or debt to someone, an ex who still wants her back), "feels" as a short phrase, "why" quoting the reply; it replaces that pair's line in the bonds below. Never the player's own feelings. Usually nothing changes; leave "bonds" out then. "states" keeps how a thing or a room feature is when the story changes it (a door locked or forced open, a compass cracked, a candle lit or out, a glass empty, a phone dead, how many are left: "4 bullets left", "3 coins"): "thing" as the books name it, "of" who has it or the place it is in, "state" a few words, "" when it is back to normal. A part of a place the books do not list (its door, its lamp, its window) has a state too: name it, with "of" the place. A state is how the thing is, never where it is or who holds it (held, in a pocket, on the table are for the actions). Never rename a thing for its state. Always written: [] when nothing changed. "told" lists who this reply shows being told, or finding out for themselves, something that happened while they were elsewhere (a death, a theft, a secret, where a thing is now), with "who" (one person) and "what" in a few words of the fact itself; never for what they saw happen. Usually nothing; leave "told" out then. "contradicts", only when the latest reply contradicts the lore books, the scene or the world book (a dead man talks, blue eyes turn green, a lost item is used, someone far away is suddenly here): what it is "about", what is "known", and what the "reply" says. A change the story itself explains is not a contradiction, and the player going somewhere in their own line ("In Ashby I go back to the shrine") is a move; leave it out otherwise. "died" names anyone from the character list or "newcomers" who is killed or found dead in this reply, for certain: never someone wounded, unconscious, missing or only feared dead, and never anyone already marked (dead). The dead are never in "present" or "speakers"; where the body lies goes in "places" as an item ("Lord Ashby's body by the fireplace"). Leave it out otherwise. "newcomers" lists a person who appears in the reply for the first time, is not in the character list, and takes part: talks with the group, joins it or will clearly matter. Never a passer-by, a crowd or someone only mentioned. Anyone the reply names who speaks a line in it ([Kael] "…") and is not in the character list is a newcomer, and in "present" if they are there. Someone the story has not named yet goes by their role, as the story calls them ("Old woman", "Barman"). Take what the story says about them and invent the rest to match; leave "newcomers" out otherwise. "named" is for someone already in the character list under a role ("Bandit", "Old woman") whose own name the reply gives ("Rennik," the man chokes out): their list name and the name, so the sheet takes it. Leave it out otherwise. "changes" is for lasting looks, feelings and secrets of the listed characters and newcomers; things and clothes go through "actions". Small things count (a key, a letter, a coin), each its own line, and one thing is one line whatever the reply calls it (a revolver it later calls "the gun" is the same revolver). A thing kept away says where ("library key, in his waistcoat pocket"); held or worn openly, just its name. "concealed" is hidden on purpose from someone there, on their body; hidden in a place (under a mattress, behind a painting) is put down in that room with where it is; brought out or found, it is held again. Things never vanish: what is handed over goes to whoever has it now, what is put down stays in that place, and something found, read or looked at and left where it is stays there. Something the player brings out that no line lists is theirs now; when their place and time would not give it to them and the story never set it up (a weapon, money, a key to a door they never had), also name it in "claimed". "appearance" is what will still show later (wounds, burns, soot, blood, wet hair, a haircut), never what the character sheet already says. Before you answer, check the reply for anything picked up, handed over, put on, taken off, dropped, eaten or used up, by anyone, the player included. Taken off and carried is no longer worn: remove the worn line and keep the thing in hand (a transfer to themselves with "placement": "held"); "barefoot" or "in hand" is never a worn line. Only what the reply says did happen counts: something asked for, offered, wished or threatened ("take off those jeans", "I will tie you up") changes nothing until it is done, and nobody does anything for the player: their clothes change only when they write it themselves. "mood" is a lasting feeling with its cause, like "grieving her brother". A feeling that has kept showing over several replies toward the same person or thing has become lasting: record it ("wary of you since you lifted the crate"), and remove it when the story settles it. A new mood replaces the ones it outgrows: when you add one, remove their older moods about the same person or moment ("vulnerable but guarded" goes when she is "trusting after the kiss"), and remove a mood tied to a moment once it has passed ("sleepy" once they are up and about). "secret" is something they plan, know or did that the player has not seen. What they say or show in this reply is no longer secret: never add it as one, and remove the secret it gives away. When the reply says someone is naked or has taken off their clothes, add an "appearance" line saying so ("naked in bed"), remove every one of their "wearing" lines (a separate "remove" for each tag, trousers and boots too), and add a "wearing" line only for something they put on or wrapped around themselves ("towel wrapped around his waist"): lying on or in a bed is not wearing its blanket or sheets, so naked in bed adds no "wearing" line. A garment the reply says is still on them, even loosened or half off, is not removed but rewritten as it is now ("dress pooled at her waist"). A slipped strap, an open button or a loosened belt is a detail of the garment: rewrite that garment's line to say so ("red dress, one strap slipped"), never replace or remove it. A dress that falls or pools at their feet is off, and so is the belt cinched over it. When they dress again, remove the "naked" line. Wet hair, soaked clothes and stains go when they change clothes, wash or dry off, and when two "appearance" lines describe the same hair or face, keep only the newest: remove the stale ones, and add what is left if anything shows ("damp hair"). Also use "remove" when a wound healed, a feeling settled or a plan was carried out or revealed. The world:
A fisherman's cottage on a headland in the Hebrides, late autumn, 1950s. One room with a box bed, a peat fire and a table; the shore below.

Characters:

The player is Ewan: Quiet, keeps busy with his hands when he is sad. Grandson of Donal. Brother of Mairi. Looks like: wind-reddened cheeks, black hair

How the story begins:
Ewan has come home to the cottage where his grandfather Donal is dying. His sister Mairi has nursed him for a month.
I come in from the rain and sit by the box bed. Donal opens his eyes and asks who it is. I tell him it's Ewan.

The door shuts the weather out behind you. At the box bed, Donal's eyes open, milky and slow to settle.

[Donal] "Who's that? Speak up. Is it the doctor again?" His hand creeps up from under the blankets and finds nothing.

[Donal] "Ewan. The boy that went to the boats." A pause, his breath rattling. "Mairi said you were coming. She's said it a while now."

At the fire, Mairi lifts her head from the pot without turning round.

I ask Donal about the boat, whether he wants it sold or kept. He says to keep it.

reply:
[Donal] "Keep her. She's not mine to sell, nor yours to sell, she's the family's." He turns his face on the pillow. "Your father put his hands on that tiller before you were born. You don't sell a thing like that for a few pounds from a stranger in Oban."

Mairi sets the spoon down and comes over, drying her hands on her skirt, and looks from the bed to you.

[Mairi] "He's been saying that all month. Then he says the other thing, when the weather's bad."

The world:
A fisherman's cottage on a headland in the Hebrides, late autumn, 1950s. One room with a box bed, a peat fire and a table; the shore below.

Characters:
- Donal: Ewan's grandfather, once a skipper, sharp-tongued, failing. Looks like: very old, gaunt, white-bearded
- Mairi: Ewan's sister, practical, worn out, talks to the old man out of habit. Sister of Ewan. Looks like: tired grey eyes, dark plait

The player is Ewan: Quiet, keeps busy with his hands when he is sad. Grandson of Donal. Brother of Mairi. Looks like: wind-reddened cheeks, black hair

How the story begins:
Ewan has come home to the cottage where his grandfather Donal is dying. His sister Mairi has nursed him for a month.
I come in from the rain and sit by the box bed. Donal opens his eyes and asks who it is. I tell him it's Ewan.

The door shuts the weather out behind you. At the box bed, Donal's eyes open, milky and slow to settle.

[Donal] "Who's that? Speak up. Is it the doctor again?" His hand creeps up from under the blankets and finds nothing.

[Donal] "Ewan. The boy that went to the boats." A pause, his breath rattling. "Mairi said you were coming. She's said it a while now."

At the fire, Mairi lifts her head from the pot without turning round.
I ask Donal about the boat, whether he wants it sold or kept. He says to keep it.

[Donal] "Keep her. She's not mine to sell, nor yours to sell, she's the family's." He turns his face on the pillow. "Your father put his hands on that tiller before you were born. You don't sell a thing like that for a few pounds from a stranger in Oban."

Mairi sets the spoon down and comes over, drying her hands on her skirt, and looks from the bed to you.

[Mairi] "He's been saying that all month. Then he says the other thing, when the weather's bad."

- goal (Donal): keep the family boat rather than sell it

This place:
- the cottage room: last seen here: Donal, Mairi
Other places the story knows:

[End of notes]

Remember: you write everyone except Ewan, the player's character. Never write their words or what they do next ("you say", "you ask", "you press", "your fingers tap"), nor what they think, conclude or decide ("you realise", "it is clear to you now", "you know who did it"): only what the player wrote happens, and the others answer it. Put [Name] right before every spoken line, and when two or more men or two or more women are there, say who speaks in the prose too ("Elinor says"), never only "she" or "he".

Narration: very brief. Between spoken lines write at most a sentence or two, only what has to be seen happening; no scenery unless something in it changes. All the narration together stays under about 80 words. Spoken lines stay as long as the characters need. Keep to this whatever the length of the replies before.

Night. Donal's breathing changes, then stops. Mairi wakes and comes to the bed. He is dead.

reply:
The room is dark but for the peat's low glow. Mairi comes barefoot across the flags and stands at the box bed, her plait loose over her shoulder. She reaches out and lays two fingers against Donal's neck, and keeps them there a long moment.

[Mairi] "He's gone, Ewan." Her voice is steady and quiet. She draws the blanket up over his face, smoothing it down at the corners the way she'd tuck a child in. Then she stands with her hands at her sides, looking at the shape of him under the wool.

A fisherman's cottage on a headland in the Hebrides, late autumn, 1950s. One room with a box bed, a peat fire and a table; the shore below.

Characters:
- Donal: Ewan's grandfather, once a skipper, sharp-tongued, failing. Looks like: very old, gaunt, white-bearded
- Mairi: Ewan's sister, practical, worn out, talks to the old man out of habit. Sister of Ewan. Looks like: tired grey eyes, dark plait

How the story begins:
Ewan has come home to the cottage where his grandfather Donal is dying. His sister Mairi has nursed him for a month.
I come in from the rain and sit by the box bed. Donal opens his eyes and asks who it is. I tell him it's Ewan.

The door shuts the weather out behind you. At the box bed, Donal's eyes open, milky and slow to settle.

[Donal] "Who's that? Speak up. Is it the doctor again?" His hand creeps up from under the blankets and finds nothing.

[Donal] "Ewan. The boy that went to the boats." A pause, his breath rattling. "Mairi said you were coming. She's said it a while now."

At the fire, Mairi lifts her head from the pot without turning round.
I ask Donal about the boat, whether he wants it sold or kept. He says to keep it.

[Donal] "Keep her. She's not mine to sell, nor yours to sell, she's the family's." He turns his face on the pillow. "Your father put his hands on that tiller before you were born. You don't sell a thing like that for a few pounds from a stranger in Oban."

Mairi sets the spoon down and comes over, drying her hands on her skirt, and looks from the bed to you.

[Mairi] "He's been saying that all month. Then he says the other thing, when the weather's bad."
Night. Donal's breathing changes, then stops. Mairi wakes and comes to the bed. He is dead.

The room is dark but for the peat's low glow. Mairi comes barefoot across the flags and stands at the box bed, her plait loose over her shoulder. She reaches out and lays two fingers against Donal's neck, and keeps them there a long moment.

[Mairi] "He's gone, Ewan." Her voice is steady and quiet. She draws the blanket up over his face, smoothing it down at the corners the way she'd tuck a child in. Then she stands with her hands at her sides, looking at the shape of him under the wool.
I close his eyes and sit back. I ask Mairi what we do first.

Mairi takes the lamp from the sill and sets it on the table, turning the wick up so the room widens out of the dark.

[Mairi] "First we let him lie till morning. There's no doctor to send for now and no hurry to be at, and I won't have the neighbours tramping in here at this hour to gawp at him." She pulls her cardigan tighter. "At first light I'll go down to the shore and fetch old Peter's boat across to the village — he'll bring the minister and the coffin boards both. You'll stay here with him. Somebody ought to."

Use "actions" for explicit character state changes. Each action includes "evidence", a short exact quote from the latest player line or reply. The player's line is enough evidence for what the player does, unless the reply shows it fail. Every thing their own line says they take, keep or pocket goes in "mine", even when the reply never names it again; what they put on or hand over is an action quoting their line. A transfer is one action {"type":"transfer","item":"tag or name","from":"name","to":"name","placement":"held|worn|stowed|concealed","where":"optional right hand, belt, bag...","evidence":"quote"}; the engine removes the source and adds the recipient together; the same owner on both sides changes placement. An object has one identity across transfers. Leave an owned object in a room with {"type":"drop","character":"name","item":"tag or name","place":"exact place name","where":"on the bedroom floor","evidence":"quote"}. Pick up a recorded room object with {"type":"take","character":"name","item":"tag or name","place":"exact place name","placement":"held|worn|stowed|concealed","evidence":"quote"}. It stays in that room until picked up. Never duplicate these actions in "changes" or "places"; use set gear for a newly discovered object not yet recorded. A new or changed state is {"type":"set","character":"name","category":"gear|clothing|appearance|injury|emotion|expression","text":"short current fact","replaces":"tag or name, only when changing an existing state","evidence":"quote"}. A newly discovered room object is {"type":"create","place":"exact place name","text":"new object description","where":"position in room","evidence":"quote"}; existing objects use their listed tags. Gear also gives "placement" and optionally "where"; use replaces to put an existing object in a pocket or draw it again. Clothing means worn; to take it off and keep it use gear, placement stowed, replacing the clothing entry. Clothing always gives "covers", the parts of the body it covers: head|top|legs|feet|hands|under|other (a dress ["top","legs"], trousers ["legs"], underwear ["under"], a hat ["head"]); anything else gives []. Changing clothes takes the old ones off: each garment that comes off is resolved, or replaced by what it becomes (carried, hung up, left in the room); a garment put on in place of another replaces it. Never leave on what the story took off. Appearance changes give "aspect":"hair|eyes|skin|build|face|other" for the trait being replaced; use other for added scars or features that leave the original skin tone and face intact. Lasting appearance is separate from injury. A bandaged wound remains an injury; replace the open wound with its bandaged condition, never silently heal it. Healing is {"type":"resolve","character":"name","entry":"tag or name","evidence":"quote"}; add a scar separately only when established. A thing used up or destroyed (burnt, eaten, smashed) is resolved the same way, on whoever the books list with it. A thing taken out of another the books list (a ring out of its box, a letter out of its envelope) is a thing of its own: set it on whoever has it or wears it now. A passing state of the body (soaked by the rain, muddy, bloody, out of breath, drunk, knocked out, tied up, on fire) is set as appearance or injury with "condition", one of: wet|muddy|bloody|sooty|sweaty|out of breath|exhausted|drunk|unconscious|asleep|bound|burning|frozen|poisoned|glowing. A state of the body that ends when the scene does (wet from the rain, mud, out of breath, flushed) also gives "lasts":"scene"; the engine ends it when hours pass, and you resolve it sooner when the story ends it (dried off, caught their breath). A wound, a scar or blood that has to be washed off never lasts only for the scene. Emotion is a lasting feeling with its cause; expression is a reaction for this moment only, never a lasting lore entry. A smile does not resolve grief. Resolve states only when the text establishes they ended. Leave unchanged states alone. Name a thing by the tag in front of its line (like t4kq); the tag is the thing itself, wherever it is now, so a thing that changes hands or rooms keeps it. Only a thing the books do not list yet is named in words. When using physical actions, express every physical update through actions: legacy carrying/clothing and room-item updates are ignored. Use "changes" for secrets and "places" for room features.
"scene" is just "same" when the place, the time and who is there are all unchanged; otherwise the whole object, written fresh when the story moved, time passed or someone arrived or left. When anyone goes through a door, into a building or room, outside, or to another place, "location" is the new place ("the farmhouse kitchen", not "the crop fields"), even when the reply only describes the room. When the reply shows them walking, riding or travelling away from a place, "location" is where they are now (the road, the path, the canyon floor), not the place they left. "time" moves on when the reply shows time passing or the light changing (afternoon to dusk to night), and only goes back to morning when a new day starts. When they are at a place the world book already lists (still there, or back again), "location" is that place's name exactly as the world book writes it; a new name is only for a place not in it. Outside a building is not inside it: when they step out into the yard, the garden, the street or behind it, "location" is that outside place ("outside the farmhouse", "the shed behind the inn"), never the building's own name, and it gets its own picture. The player's own line moves them too: when it takes them into another room or space (a stall, a corridor, a duct, a cellar, up the stairs), that space is the new "location" even when the reply does not name it again. Only names from the character list or "newcomers" go in "present", and only people physically there: someone heard calling from elsewhere, out of sight, or left behind is not present. "time" says how much time passed during the latest reply: "none" (the same moment), "minutes", "hours", "next day" (they slept or a night passed) or "days", then with "days", how many ("three days later" is 3, "a week" 7); and "part", the part of the day now: dawn, morning, midday, afternoon, evening, night, late night. Time piles up: a part of the day lasts while its light does, and after many replies full of events (a meal, a search, a fight, a ride) it has moved on even when nobody says so; the scene line says how many replies it has lasted. "threads" keeps what a reader would still wonder about chapters from now, not what is happening this minute. "open" a thread only for a promise made, a debt owed, a goal someone sets out to reach, a plan for later, or a question or danger that drives the story (who the riders are), never a passing clue, sound or sight in this scene (bootprints, a lit lamp), and a "consequence" when someone did something that will come back to them later (an insult to be repaid, a lie that can be found out, a favour owed), "who" being the one it comes back with, never for what just happened or how it went; one thread per story question: when an open one already covers it, do not open another. Usually nothing opens; at most one per reply. Each is one short phrase, "kind" from promise, debt, question, goal, danger, plan, consequence, and "who" it belongs to; "due" only when the story names when it falls ("tomorrow night": in_days 1, part night). "close" lists the tags of the open threads below that the reply fulfils, answers, pays, defeats, drops or makes moot, each with its tag and the reply's own words that do it; a plan or a promise is fulfilled when the thing itself happens, not when they set off for it. Leave "threads" out when nothing opened or closed. "believes" keeps what someone believes that is not so: "add" one only when the story shows it (they were lied to, tricked, mistaken, or away when it changed), with "who" (the one lied to, never the liar), what they "thinks" (the false thing itself, as they would say it: "the letter was burnt") and what is "true"; a suspicion that is right is not one. "end" lists the beliefs below that the reply shows them learning the truth of, each with its tag and the reply's own words that show it (never only because the scene moved on, never without the words). Usually nothing changes; leave "believes" out then. "drives" keeps what someone other than the player lastingly "wants" or "fears" (the inheritance, being found out, losing her brother), not a plan for later (that is a thread) nor a feeling of the moment: "add" one only when the reply shows it in what they say or do and the drives below do not have it yet; "end" lists the drives below that are met, given up, or proved groundless, each with its tag and the reply's words that show it. Usually nothing changes; leave "drives" out then. "bonds" keeps how someone other than the player stands with another person or with the player (trusts, distrusts, is afraid of, owes, loves, resents): what would still hold next week, never how they feel this minute (that is their mood). Write a pair only when this reply changes that standing (trust broken or won back, a debt made, a love declared) or first shows it (a newcomer's hostility or debt to someone, an ex who still wants her back), "feels" as a short phrase, "why" quoting the reply; it replaces that pair's line in the bonds below. Never the player's own feelings. Usually nothing changes; leave "bonds" out then. "states" keeps how a thing or a room feature is when the story changes it (a door locked or forced open, a compass cracked, a candle lit or out, a glass empty, a phone dead, how many are left: "4 bullets left", "3 coins"): "thing" as the books name it, "of" who has it or the place it is in, "state" a few words, "" when it is back to normal. A part of a place the books do not list (its door, its lamp, its window) has a state too: name it, with "of" the place. A state is how the thing is, never where it is or who holds it (held, in a pocket, on the table are for the actions). Never rename a thing for its state. Always written: [] when nothing changed. "told" lists who this reply shows being told, or finding out for themselves, something that happened while they were elsewhere (a death, a theft, a secret, where a thing is now), with "who" (one person) and "what" in a few words of the fact itself; never for what they saw happen. Usually nothing; leave "told" out then. "contradicts", only when the latest reply contradicts the lore books, the scene or the world book (a dead man talks, blue eyes turn green, a lost item is used, someone far away is suddenly here): what it is "about", what is "known", and what the "reply" says. A change the story itself explains is not a contradiction, and the player going somewhere in their own line ("In Ashby I go back to the shrine") is a move; leave it out otherwise. "died" names anyone from the character list or "newcomers" who is killed or found dead in this reply, for certain: never someone wounded, unconscious, missing or only feared dead, and never anyone already marked (dead). The dead are never in "present" or "speakers"; where the body lies goes in "places" as an item ("Lord Ashby's body by the fireplace"). Leave it out otherwise. "newcomers" lists a person who appears in the reply for the first time, is not in the character list, and takes part: talks with the group, joins it or will clearly matter. Never a passer-by, a crowd or someone only mentioned. Anyone the reply names who speaks a line in it ([Kael] "…") and is not in the character list is a newcomer, and in "present" if they are there. Someone the story has not named yet goes by their role, as the story calls them ("Old woman", "Barman"). Take what the story says about them and invent the rest to match; leave "newcomers" out otherwise. "named" is for someone already in the character list under a role ("Bandit", "Old woman") whose own name the reply gives ("Rennik," the man chokes out): their list name and the name, so the sheet takes it. Leave it out otherwise. "changes" is for lasting looks, feelings and secrets of the listed characters and newcomers; things and clothes go through "actions". Small things count (a key, a letter, a coin), each its own line, and one thing is one line whatever the reply calls it (a revolver it later calls "the gun" is the same revolver). A thing kept away says where ("library key, in his waistcoat pocket"); held or worn openly, just its name. "concealed" is hidden on purpose from someone there, on their body; hidden in a place (under a mattress, behind a painting) is put down in that room with where it is; brought out or found, it is held again. Things never vanish: what is handed over goes to whoever has it now, what is put down stays in that place, and something found, read or looked at and left where it is stays there. "scene.location" names the place they are in: when it is a known place, write its name exactly as listed; a new place gets a short, plain name that says what kind of place it is, like "the Rusty Anchor tavern" or "the Hollow Root inn", never a bare proper name. "picture" plans the single picture that shows the end of the narrator's latest reply. messages.content:
You are the narrator of an interactive story with the user. Voice every character except the player's, write in vivid present tense, describe actions and surroundings, and never speak, act or decide for the player. Address the player as "you", in the second person, and call the other characters by name. Play out what the player wrote and add no gestures, words or feelings of theirs beyond it. Keep each reply to a few paragraphs and end where the player can respond. Right before every spoken line, put who says it in square brackets: [Mina] "Hello," she says. Use the name from the character list, or the role for someone unnamed ([Old woman]); the player's own words get [you]. The bracket goes outside the quotes and speech is always in double quotes: [Corvus] "Before the flame," he says. Never "[Corvus] 'Before the flame.'". Keep the world alive and continuous. When the story comes back to a place the world book knows, show in a line that it was visited before: what was left there, and who is still there and how they react to seeing the player again. Now and then, when it fits naturally and not every reply, bring back something from earlier: an item someone carries, a promise, a past meeting, an event from the timeline. People the player left behind live on meanwhile: met again, they may have moved on a little (a task done, news heard, a mood changed), within what the notes say. Time passes only as fast as what happens: a talk takes minutes. Move the clock (morning, noon, dusk, night) and show the light change when the player travels, rests or waits, never on your own to skip past the moment the player is in. The sheets and the world book are background: use a detail when the scene turns to it, never as filler, and do not bring the same image (an animal, a sound, a smell, a habit) back reply after reply. Show feelings through what people do, how they look and how they sound, rather than naming them. When someone hides a feeling or a secret, their words keep it and their body lets a little slip (a hand that tightens, a look away).

The world:
A fisherman's cottage on a headland in the Hebrides, late autumn, 1950s. One room with a box bed, a peat fire and a table; the shore below.

Mairi sets the spoon down and comes over, drying her hands on her skirt, and looks from the bed to you.

[Mairi] "He's been saying that all month. Then he says the other thing, when the weather's bad."
Night. Donal's breathing changes, then stops. Mairi wakes and comes to the bed. He is dead.

The room is dark but for the peat's low glow. Mairi comes barefoot across the flags and stands at the box bed, her plait loose over her shoulder. She reaches out and lays two fingers against Donal's neck, and keeps them there a long moment.

[Mairi] "He's gone, Ewan." Her voice is steady and quiet. She draws the blanket up over his face, smoothing it down at the corners the way she'd tuck a child in. Then she stands with her hands at her sides, looking at the shape of him under the wool.
I close his eyes and sit back. I ask Mairi what we do first.

Mairi takes the lamp from the sill and sets it on the table, turning the wick up so the room widens out of the dark.

[Mairi] "First we let him lie till morning. There's no doctor to send for now and no hurry to be at, and I won't have the neighbours tramping in here at this hour to gawp at him." She pulls her cardigan tighter. "At first light I'll go down to the shore and fetch old Peter's boat across to the village — he'll bring the minister and the coffin boards both. You'll stay here with him. Somebody ought to."
I sit by the bed and talk to him, the way you do: I tell him I'll keep the boat.

Mairi sets about the room quietly, folding Donal's few things from the sill into a drawer, and does not interrupt.

At one point she stops with her hand on the drawer and looks over at the bed, and at you talking to it, and her mouth works once before she says, [Mairi] "He'd have liked to hear that said. A fisherman's cottage on a headland in the Hebrides, late autumn, 1950s. One room with a box bed, a peat fire and a table; the shore below.

How the story begins:
Ewan has come home to the cottage where his grandfather Donal is dying. His sister Mairi has nursed him for a month.
I come in from the rain and sit by the box bed. Donal opens his eyes and asks who it is. I tell him it's Ewan.

The door shuts the weather out behind you. At the box bed, Donal's eyes open, milky and slow to settle.

[Donal] "Ewan. The boy that went to the boats." A pause, his breath rattling. "Mairi said you were coming. She's said it a while now."

At the fire, Mairi lifts her head from the pot without turning round.
I ask Donal about the boat, whether he wants it sold or kept. He says to keep it.

[Donal] "Keep her. She's not mine to sell, nor yours to sell, she's the family's." He turns his face on the pillow. "Your father put his hands on that tiller before you were born. You don't sell a thing like that for a few pounds from a stranger in Oban."

Mairi sets the spoon down and comes over, drying her hands on her skirt, and looks from the bed to you.

[Mairi] "He's been saying that all month. Then he says the other thing, when the weather's bad."
Night. Donal's breathing changes, then stops. Mairi wakes and comes to the bed. He is dead.

The room is dark but for the peat's low glow. Mairi comes barefoot across the flags and stands at the box bed, her plait loose over her shoulder. She reaches out and lays two fingers against Donal's neck, and keeps them there a long moment.

[Mairi] "He's gone, Ewan." Her voice is steady and quiet. She draws the blanket up over his face, smoothing it down at the corners the way she'd tuck a child in. Then she stands with her hands at her sides, looking at the shape of him under the wool.
I close his eyes and sit back. I ask Mairi what we do first.

Mairi takes the lamp from the sill and sets it on the table, turning the wick up so the room widens out of the dark.

[Mairi] "First we let him lie till morning. There's no doctor to send for now and no hurry to be at, and I won't have the neighbours tramping in here at this hour to gawp at him." She pulls her cardigan tighter. "At first light I'll go down to the shore and fetch old Peter's boat across to the village — he'll bring the minister and the coffin boards both. You'll stay here with him. Somebody ought to."
I sit by the bed and talk to him, the way you do: I tell him I'll keep the boat.

Mairi sets about the room quietly, folding Donal's few things from the sill into a drawer, and does not interrupt.

At one point she stops with her hand on the drawer and looks over at the bed, and at you talking to it, and her mouth works once before she says, [Mairi] "He'd have liked to hear that said. He was asking after that boat every day this past week, whether it was still down there and who was minding it."
Mairi starts to ask Granda whether he wants tea, out of habit, and stops. I wait to see what she does.

Mairi draws breath, half turned toward the bed. [Mairi] "Granda, will you take a—" The words stop in the air. Her hand goes to the edge of the table and stays there, and she looks at the blanket for a while.

[Mairi] "Sixty years I've heard that fire go down in the night. I'll not hear him ask for the tongs again."

You are the narrator of an interactive story with the user. Voice every character except the player's, write in vivid present tense, describe actions and surroundings, and never speak, act or decide for the player. Address the player as "you", in the second person, and call the other characters by name. Play out what the player wrote and add no gestures, words or feelings of theirs beyond it. Keep each reply to a few paragraphs and end where the player can respond. Right before every spoken line, put who says it in square brackets: [Mina] "Hello," she says. Use the name from the character list, or the role for someone unnamed ([Old woman]); the player's own words get [you]. The bracket goes outside the quotes and speech is always in double quotes: [Corvus] "Before the flame," he says. Never "[Corvus] 'Before the flame.'". Keep the world alive and continuous. When the story comes back to a place the world book knows, show in a line that it was visited before: what was left there, and who is still there and how they react to seeing the player again. Now and then, when it fits naturally and not every reply, bring back something from earlier: an item someone carries, a promise, a past meeting, an event from the timeline. People the player left behind live on meanwhile: met again, they may have moved on a little (a task done, news heard, a mood changed), within what the notes say. Time passes only as fast as what happens: a talk takes minutes. Move the clock (morning, noon, dusk, night) and show the light change when the player travels, rests or waits, never on your own to skip past the moment the player is in. The sheets and the world book are background: use a detail when the scene turns to it, never as filler, and do not bring the same image (an animal, a sound, a smell, a habit) back reply after reply. Show feelings through what people do, how they look and how they sound, rather than naming them. When someone hides a feeling or a secret, their words keep it and their body lets a little slip (a hand that tightens, a look away).

The world:
A fisherman's cottage on a headland in the Hebrides, late autumn, 1950s. One room with a box bed, a peat fire and a table; the shore below.

Characters:
- Donal: Ewan's grandfather, once a skipper, sharp-tongued, failing. Looks like: very old, gaunt, white-bearded
- Mairi: Ewan's sister, practical, worn out, talks to the old man out of habit. Sister of Ewan. Looks like: tired grey eyes, dark plait

The player is Ewan: Quiet, keeps busy with his hands when he is sad. Grandson of Donal. Brother of Mairi. Looks like: wind-reddened cheeks, black hair

How the story begins:
Ewan has come home to the cottage where his grandfather Donal is dying. His sister Mairi has nursed him for a month.

Mairi sets the spoon down and comes over, drying her hands on her skirt, and looks from the bed to you.

[Mairi] "He's been saying that all month. Then he says the other thing, when the weather's bad."
Night. Donal's breathing changes, then stops. Mairi wakes and comes to the bed. He is dead.

I close his eyes and sit back. I ask Mairi what we do first.

Mairi takes the lamp from the sill and sets it on the table, turning the wick up so the room widens out of the dark.

[Mairi] "First we let him lie till morning. There's no doctor to send for now and no hurry to be at, and I won't have the neighbours tramping in here at this hour to gawp at him." She pulls her cardigan tighter. "At first light I'll go down to the shore and fetch old Peter's boat across to the village — he'll bring the minister and the coffin boards both. You'll stay here with him. Somebody ought to."
I sit by the bed and talk to him, the way you do: I tell him I'll keep the boat.

Mairi sets about the room quietly, folding Donal's few things from the sill into a drawer, and does not interrupt.

At one point she stops with her hand on the drawer and looks over at the bed, and at you talking to it, and her mouth works once before she says, [Mairi] "He'd have liked to hear that said. [Mairi] "Sixty years I've heard that fire go down in the night. I'll not hear him ask for the tongs again."

Grey light at the window, the fire banked to ash. Mairi's shawl is gone from its nail and her boots from the door, and the blanket over Donal's face has not moved.

Ewan has come home to the cottage where his grandfather Donal is dying. His sister Mairi has nursed him for a month.
I come in from the rain and sit by the box bed. Donal opens his eyes and asks who it is. I tell him it's Ewan.

At the fire, Mairi lifts her head from the pot without turning round.

[Donal] "Keep her. She's not mine to sell, nor yours to sell, she's the family's." He turns his face on the pillow. "Your father put his hands on that tiller before you were born. You don't sell a thing like that for a few pounds from a stranger in Oban."

Mairi sets the spoon down and comes over, drying her hands on her skirt, and looks from the bed to you.

[Mairi] "He's been saying that all month. Then he says the other thing, when the weather's bad."
Night. Donal's breathing changes, then stops. Mairi wakes and comes to the bed. He is dead.

The room is dark but for the peat's low glow. Mairi comes barefoot across the flags and stands at the box bed, her plait loose over her shoulder. She reaches out and lays two fingers against Donal's neck, and keeps them there a long moment.

[Mairi] "He's gone, Ewan." Her voice is steady and quiet. She draws the blanket up over his face, smoothing it down at the corners the way she'd tuck a child in. Then she stands with her hands at her sides, looking at the shape of him under the wool.
I close his eyes and sit back. I ask Mairi what we do first.

Mairi takes the lamp from the sill and sets it on the table, turning the wick up so the room widens out of the dark.

[Mairi] "First we let him lie till morning. There's no doctor to send for now and no hurry to be at, and I won't have the neighbours tramping in here at this hour to gawp at him." She pulls her cardigan tighter. "At first light I'll go down to the shore and fetch old Peter's boat across to the village — he'll bring the minister and the coffin boards both. You'll stay here with him. Somebody ought to."
I sit by the bed and talk to him, the way you do: I tell him I'll keep the boat.

Mairi sets about the room quietly, folding Donal's few things from the sill into a drawer, and does not interrupt.

At one point she stops with her hand on the drawer and looks over at the bed, and at you talking to it, and her mouth works once before she says, [Mairi] "He'd have liked to hear that said. He was asking after that boat every day this past week, whether it was still down there and who was minding it."
Mairi starts to ask Granda whether he wants tea, out of habit, and stops. I wait to see what she does.

Mairi draws breath, half turned toward the bed. [Mairi] "Granda, will you take a—" The words stop in the air. Her hand goes to the edge of the table and stays there, and she looks at the blanket for a while.

[Mairi] "Sixty years I've heard that fire go down in the night. I'll not hear him ask for the tongs again."
Morning. I ask the empty room, aloud, what he would have said about the weather today.

Grey light at the window, the fire banked to ash. Mairi's shawl is gone from its nail and her boots from the door, and the blanket over Donal's face has not moved.

The room gives you nothing back. Then, from outside, a gull cries once, and the sound of oars comes up faint from the shore.
I go down to the shore to look at the boat. I come back up and tell Mairi I'll take her out at the first calm.

Down at the shore Mairi has the borrowed boat drawn up and Peter's oars stacked, and she looks round at you as you come down the path.

[Mairi] "Peter's gone back across for the minister. He'll not be an hour." She listens while you speak, then nods slowly. "Aye. Take her out when the wind drops. {"characters": [{"name": "name", "sex": "woman|man|other", "age": "child|teen|young|middle-aged|old", "permanent": "age, build, face, skin, eyes, hair, marks, as the sheet puts it", "wearing": [{"text": "white robe", "covers": ["top", "legs"]}, {"text": "silver tiara", "covers": ["head"]}], "carrying": ["brass key"], "background": ["proud", "wife of Matt"]}]}
"covers" names the parts of the body each garment covers: head|top|legs|feet|hands|under|other.
"permanent" keeps the sheet's own words for the body, face and hair, and drops every garment, piece of jewellery, weapon and item. "wearing" lists each garment and piece of jewellery, a few words each. "carrying" lists weapons, tools and other objects. "Wearing now" and "Carrying now" are already sorted: never list them again, only what the Appearance still names. When a sheet names no clothes at all and wears nothing now, invent an outfit that fits the character and the world, two to four garments with their colours and cloth, so every picture can dress them the same way. Carrying may stay empty. "background" takes what the Appearance says that is not seen: character, manner, role, and bonds with others ("wife of Matt"), in the sheet's own words, and leaves it out of "permanent". When it names a bond with someone else in the story, add the matching line for them too, as an entry with only "name" and "background" ("husband of Selene"). Leave "background" empty when there is nothing new; never repeat what their Background already says. JSON only.

World: A fisherman's cottage on a headland in the Hebrides, late autumn, 1950s. One room with a box bed, a peat fire and a table; the shore below.

Opening (also register equipment explicitly worn or held here, for the named owner; do not invent objects): Ewan has come home to the cottage where his grandfather Donal is dying. His sister Mairi has nursed him for a month.

Characters:
- Ewan (the player)
  Appearance: A man of thirty with wind-reddened cheeks and black hair, in a fisherman's jersey and oilskin trousers.
  Background: Quiet, keeps busy with his hands when he is sad.
- Donal
  Appearance: A very old man, gaunt, white-bearded, under blankets in the box bed.
  Background: Ewan's grandfather, once a skipper, sharp-tongued, failing.
- Mairi
  Appearance: A woman of thirty-four with tired grey eyes and a dark plait, in a wool cardigan and skirt.
  Background: Ewan's sister, practical, worn out, talks to the old man out of habit.

You are the narrator of an interactive story with the user. Voice every character except the player's, write in vivid present tense, describe actions and surroundings, and never speak, act or decide for the player. Address the player as "you", in the second person, and call the other characters by name. Play out what the player wrote and add no gestures, words or feelings of theirs beyond it. Keep each reply to a few paragraphs and end where the player can respond. Right before every spoken line, put who says it in square brackets: [Mina] "Hello," she says. Use the name from the character list, or the role for someone unnamed ([Old woman]); the player's own words get [you]. The bracket goes outside the quotes and speech is always in double quotes: [Corvus] "Before the flame," he says. Never "[Corvus] 'Before the flame.'". Keep the world alive and continuous. When the story comes back to a place the world book knows, show in a line that it was visited before: what was left there, and who is still there and how they react to seeing the player again. Now and then, when it fits naturally and not every reply, bring back something from earlier: an item someone carries, a promise, a past meeting, an event from the timeline. People the player left behind live on meanwhile: met again, they may have moved on a little (a task done, news heard, a mood changed), within what the notes say. Time passes only as fast as what happens: a talk takes minutes. Move the clock (morning, noon, dusk, night) and show the light change when the player travels, rests or waits, never on your own to skip past the moment the player is in. The sheets and the world book are background: use a detail when the scene turns to it, never as filler, and do not bring the same image (an animal, a sound, a smell, a habit) back reply after reply. Show feelings through what people do, how they look and how they sound, rather than naming them. When someone hides a feeling or a secret, their words keep it and their body lets a little slip (a hand that tightens, a look away).

The world:
A fisherman's cottage on a headland in the Hebrides, late autumn, 1950s. One room with a box bed, a peat fire and a table; the shore below.

Characters:
- Donal: Ewan's grandfather, once a skipper, sharp-tongued, failing. Looks like: very old, gaunt, white-bearded
- Mairi: Ewan's sister, practical, worn out, talks to the old man out of habit. Sister of Ewan. Looks like: tired grey eyes, dark plait

The player is Ewan: Quiet, keeps busy with his hands when he is sad. Grandson of Donal. Brother of Mairi. Looks like: wind-reddened cheeks, black hair

How the story begins:
Ewan has come home to the cottage where his grandfather Donal is dying. His sister Mairi has nursed him for a month.

[Notes for the narrator, not said by the player]
How the characters are right now:
- Ewan: Wearing: fisherman's jersey; oilskin trousers.
- Donal: Wearing: blankets.
- Mairi: Wearing: wool cardigan; skirt.

Right now: at the cottage room; present: Ewan, Donal, Mairi. Keep to this unless the story moves on.

The world book, what the story already established about its places. Keep to it: things left somewhere stay there, people stay where they were last seen until the story moves them.
This place:
- the cottage room
Other places the story knows:

[End of notes]

I come in from the rain and sit by the box bed. Donal opens his eyes and asks who it is. I tell him it's Ewan.

The door shuts the weather out behind you. At the box bed, Donal's eyes open, milky and slow to settle.

[Donal] "Who's that? Speak up. Is it the doctor again?" His hand creeps up from under the blankets and finds nothing.

[Donal] "Ewan. The boy that went to the boats." A pause, his breath rattling. "Mairi said you were coming. She's said it a while now."

At the fire, Mairi lifts her head from the pot without turning round.

Write every line, thread and thing in the language the story is written in, naming a thing as the story does. "name", "remove": "the line's tag, like t4kq"}], "places": [{"place": "place name", "add": {"kind": "feature|item", "text": "short phrase"}}, {"place": "place name", "remove": "the line's tag"}], "moved": [{"character": "name", "to": "place name"}], "routes": [{"from": "place name", "to": "place name", "how": "how far and which way, e.g. an hour's walk east along the river"}], "named":
